questions.stem: The sugar, oil and egg in a chef's kitchen are all made of biomolecules. Which element forms the backbone of all of them?
questions.explanation: Carbon makes four covalent bonds, so it can form long chains and rings.

questions.stem: The egg white you whisk is mostly protein. What are the monomers (building blocks) of a protein?
questions.explanation: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

questions.stem: Which element is found in proteins and nucleic acids but not in carbohydrates or triglycerides?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates and triglycerides contain only C, H and O. Amino acids and nucleotide bases contain N.

questions.stem: A swimmer eats pasta the night before a race. Pasta is rich in starch. Digestion breaks starch down into:
questions.explanation: Starch is a polymer of glucose, so digestion gives glucose.

questions.stem: A DNA sample has 30% adenine. What percent of the bases are guanine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T, so T = 30%. A + T = 60%, leaving 40% for G + C. G = C = 20%.

questions.stem: Cooking an egg turns the clear egg white solid and white. Which statement best explains this?

choices.A: Heat unfolds (denatures) the proteins, which clump together; the amino acid sequence is unchanged.
choices.B: Heat adds new amino acids to the protein chains.
choices.C: Heat changes the protein into starch.
choices.D: Heat breaks every peptide bond, so the protein becomes free amino acids.
choices.E: Heat removes the carbon atoms from the proteins.

questions.explanation: Mild heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the 3D shape. The peptide bonds (primary structure) stay intact.

questions.stem: Which description fits a triglyceride?

choices.A: Three glucose molecules joined to one glycerol
choices.B: One glycerol joined to two fatty acids and a phosphate group
choices.C: One glycerol joined to three fatty acids
choices.D: Three glycerol molecules joined to one fatty acid
choices.E: One glycerol joined to three amino acids

questions.explanation: A triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids. The option with a phosphate group describes a phospholipid.

questions.stem: A polypeptide is built from 12 amino acids in one chain. How many peptide bonds does it contain, and how many water molecules were released making it?
questions.explanation: Joining n amino acids in a chain makes n − 1 bonds, and each bond releases one water: 12 − 1 = 11.

questions.stem: Which shows the flow of information in the central dogma?
questions.explanation: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.

questions.stem: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil (U) where DNA uses thymine (T).

questions.stem: In a team analogy, the coach's play (mRNA) is carried out by the players. In a cell, where does translation take place?

choices.A: At a ribosome in the cytoplasm

questions.explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA codons and build the polypeptide.

questions.stem: A team's coach keeps the master playbook (the DNA) in the office and sends a copy of just one play to the players. What is this copying process, and what is the copy?
questions.explanation: Making an RNA copy of one gene is transcription, and the working copy is mRNA. The difference: the DNA playbook itself is never used up or moved.

questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TAC GGA CTT-5′. What is the mRNA made from it (written 5′ to 3′)?
questions.explanation: Pair each template base: T→A, A→U, C→G gives AUG, then G→C, G→C, A→U gives CCU, then C→G, T→A, T→A gives GAA. RNA has U, not T.

questions.stem: A eukaryotic gene has 3 exons and 2 introns. What does the mature mRNA contain?

choices.A: The 3 exons and 2 introns, without a cap or tail
choices.E: The 3 exons joined together, plus a 5′ cap and poly-A tail

questions.explanation: Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons. The cap and tail are added during processing.

questions.stem: A coding region of mRNA runs from the start codon up to (but not including) the stop codon and is 90 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
questions.explanation: Each amino acid needs one codon of 3 nucleotides: 90 ÷ 3 = 30. The stop codon does not add an amino acid.

questions.stem: DNA with both strands labeled with heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) replicates once in light nitrogen (¹⁴N). Each new DNA molecule contains:

choices.A: one heavy strand and one light strand
choices.D: one all-heavy molecule and one all-light molecule
choices.E: short heavy and light pieces mixed in both strands

questions.explanation: Replication is semi-conservative: each molecule keeps one old (heavy) strand and gets one new (light) strand.

questions.stem: Which statement is part of the cell theory?

choices.B: Cells can arise from non-living matter.
choices.D: Only plants are made of cells.
choices.E: All living things are made of one or more cells.

questions.explanation: The cell theory: living things are made of cells, the cell is the unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells.

questions.stem: A team's energy supplier keeps the credits flowing. In an animal cell, which organelle is the main site of ATP production?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration in mitochondria makes most of the ATP.

questions.stem: A cook compares a spinach leaf cell with a chicken muscle cell. Which structure is found in the plant cell but NOT in the animal cell?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts (with cell wall and a large vacuole) are typical of plant cells.

questions.stem: In a kitchen delivery service, the packing station sorts and wraps orders and sends them out. Which organelle does the same job for proteins?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles. The difference: the Golgi does not make the proteins; ribosomes do.

questions.stem: Through a microscope with a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective, a cell's image is 6 mm long. What is the real length of the cell?
questions.explanation: Total magnification = 10 × 40 = 400. Real size = image size ÷ magnification = 6 mm ÷ 400 = 0.015 mm = 15 µm.

questions.stem: A 5-agent team has each agent doing a specialist job in a different spot. In a eukaryotic cell, the matching idea (compartmentalization into organelles) is useful mainly because:

choices.A: it stops the cell from using energy
choices.C: different reactions can run at the same time under their own conditions without interfering
choices.D: it forces all reactions to occur at the same pH
choices.E: it removes the need for DNA

questions.explanation: Membrane-bound compartments keep enzymes and conditions separate, so many reactions can occur at once.

questions.stem: Which structure do bacteria and plant cells share but animal cells lack?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and plants have cell walls (different materials). Bacteria have no chloroplast, nucleus, mitochondria or ER.

questions.stem: A student draws a plant cell 45 mm long. The real cell is 0.09 mm long. What is the magnification of the drawing?
questions.explanation: Magnification = drawing size ÷ real size = 45 ÷ 0.09 = 500.

questions.stem: In which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes line up at the middle of the cell?
questions.explanation: At metaphase the chromosomes sit on the equator.

questions.stem: A swimmer's skin cell divides by mitosis. How many daughter cells does one complete mitosis plus cell division produce?
questions.explanation: Mitosis gives two identical daughter cells.

questions.stem: Meiosis produces cells that are:
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles genes (crossing over, independent assortment).

questions.stem: Swimming practice makes a swimmer's muscles grow and repair; new cells come from mitosis. What is pulled apart during anaphase of mitosis?
questions.explanation: Anaphase separates the two sister chromatids of each chromosome to opposite poles.

questions.stem: A swimmer's body cells have 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in one of her egg cells?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid (n = 23); body cells are diploid (2n = 46).

questions.stem: Which event happens in meiosis but NOT in mitosis?

choices.D: Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange pieces

questions.explanation: Pairing and crossing over of homologous chromosomes occurs only in prophase I of meiosis.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 8 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. How many cells result, and how many chromosomes does each have?
questions.explanation: Two divisions give 4 cells. The chromosome number is halved: 8 ÷ 2 = 4.

questions.stem: At the end of meiosis I, each cell has:

choices.A: a quarter of the chromosomes, each of two chromatids
choices.B: half the chromosomes, each made of one chromatid
choices.C: the full number of chromosomes, each of one chromatid
choices.D: the full number of chromosomes, each of two chromatids
choices.E: half the chromosomes, each still made of two chromatids

questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs (halving the number). Sister chromatids separate only in meiosis II.

questions.stem: A basil plant on a kitchen windowsill photosynthesizes. Which gas does it release as a by-product?
questions.explanation: Water is split and oxygen is released.

questions.stem: Which pigment absorbs light energy for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs red and blue light.

questions.stem: A pool left uncovered in summer turns green because algae grow in it. Which raw materials do the algae use for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light.

questions.stem: A cook keeps one basil plant on a sunny windowsill and another in a dark cupboard for two weeks. The one in the dark does badly mainly because:

choices.A: it has too much carbon dioxide
choices.E: without light it cannot photosynthesize to make glucose

questions.explanation: Light is needed to make glucose. Without it the plant uses up stored food and weakens.

questions.stem: In the starch test, why is the leaf warmed in ethanol before adding iodine?

choices.A: To remove the green chlorophyll so the iodine color can be seen
choices.B: To increase the rate of photosynthesis
choices.C: To add oxygen to the leaf
choices.D: To dissolve the starch out of the leaf
choices.E: To make more starch in the leaf

questions.explanation: Chlorophyll would hide the blue-black color. Boiling in water first kills the leaf and softens it.

questions.stem: A cook grows a variegated mint plant (green and white patches) in bright light, then a leaf is tested for starch. Where does the iodine turn blue-black?
questions.explanation: Only the parts with chlorophyll can photosynthesize and make starch.

questions.stem: The rate of photosynthesis rises with light, then levels off. Increasing the carbon dioxide concentration lifts the level-off point. At the original plateau, which factor was limiting?

choices.E: The amount of water in the air

questions.explanation: If adding a factor raises the plateau, that factor was limiting. More light would not help, because light was already plentiful.

questions.stem: A plant takes in 3 mol of CO₂ for photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂). How much glucose and O₂ does it make?
questions.explanation: Scale the equation by 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5: 6CO₂ makes 1 glucose, so 3CO₂ makes 0.5 glucose; 6O₂ becomes 3 O₂.

questions.stem: Which equation represents aerobic respiration?

choices.D: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases CO₂, water and a lot of energy.

questions.stem: Yeast in bread dough respires without oxygen (fermentation). Which two products make the dough rise and give the smell?
questions.explanation: Yeast makes ethanol and CO₂. The CO₂ gas bubbles make the dough rise.

questions.stem: During a long swim, a swimmer's muscle cells need lots of ATP. Where in a cell does most aerobic respiration happen?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria make most ATP using oxygen.

questions.stem: In a 50 m sprint a swimmer's muscles run short of oxygen and switch to anaerobic respiration. Which product builds up in the muscles?
questions.explanation: Animal cells make lactic acid when respiring anaerobically. Yeast makes ethanol instead.

questions.stem: How does the energy yield of aerobic respiration compare with anaerobic respiration from the same glucose?

choices.B: Aerobic gives 2 ATP and anaerobic gives 30
choices.E: Aerobic gives many more ATP (about 30 versus 2)

questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration only partly breaks down glucose, so much less energy is released.

questions.stem: Which statement about respiration in plants is correct?

choices.B: Plants only photosynthesize and never respire
choices.D: Plants respire all the time, day and night

questions.explanation: Every living cell respires continually; photosynthesis happens only in light.

questions.stem: A potted plant sits in a sealed, transparent chamber kept in the dark. After some hours, the CO₂ level in the chamber has:

choices.A: increased, because respiration continues but photosynthesis has stopped
choices.B: decreased, because plants make O₂ in the dark
choices.C: stayed the same, because plants do not respire
choices.D: decreased, because plants take in CO₂ in the dark
choices.E: increased, because plants make CO₂ by photosynthesis

questions.explanation: In the dark there is no photosynthesis to use CO₂, while respiration keeps releasing it.

questions.stem: How many moles of O₂ are needed to respire 2 mol of glucose completely (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O)?
questions.explanation: Each glucose needs 6 O₂, so 2 mol needs 2 × 6 = 12 mol.

questions.stem: Which tissue joins a muscle to a bone?
questions.explanation: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.

questions.stem: Chewed food is pushed along the intestine by slow waves of squeezing. Which muscle type is found in the intestine walls?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle is involuntary and moves food along the gut.

questions.stem: Your ear and the tip of your nose are firm but bendable. Which tissue gives them this property?
questions.explanation: Cartilage is firm yet flexible.

questions.stem: A swimmer kicks hard. Which tissue joins the thigh muscle to the shin bone, and which joins the thigh bone to the shin bone at the knee?

choices.A: Ligament joins muscle to bone; tendon joins bone to bone
choices.B: Cartilage joins muscle to bone; tendon joins bone to bone
choices.C: Tendon joins muscle to bone; ligament joins bone to bone
choices.D: Tendon joins muscle to bone; cartilage joins bone to bone
choices.E: Ligament joins both muscle to bone and bone to bone

questions.explanation: Tendon = muscle to bone. Ligament = bone to bone.

questions.stem: A cook slices a steak. The red meat is mainly which tissue?
questions.explanation: Meat is skeletal muscle from the animal's body.

questions.stem: What is the main role of epithelial tissue?

choices.A: To contract and move the bones
choices.C: To carry oxygen around the body
choices.D: To cover body surfaces and line organs and cavities as a protective layer
choices.E: To store calcium and support the body

questions.explanation: Epithelium forms the skin surface and lines organs such as the gut.

questions.stem: Which description matches cardiac muscle?

choices.A: Long striated fibers with many nuclei, attached to bones
choices.B: Spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus each, not striated, voluntary
choices.C: Branched cells without stripes, contracting voluntarily
choices.D: Spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus each, not striated, involuntary
choices.E: Branched, striated cells joined by intercalated discs, contracting involuntarily

questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart; the intercalated discs link the cells together.

questions.stem: Which pairing of tissue and feature is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle is NOT striated and is involuntary. All other pairings are correct.

questions.stem: A chef uses a degreaser on oily pans; the body's 'degreaser' for fat is bile. Which organ makes bile?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder only stores it.

questions.stem: A swimmer eats a banana after training. Where does most absorption of digested food take place?
questions.explanation: The small intestine has villi that give a large surface area.

questions.stem: A slice of bread tastes slightly sweet after you chew it for a minute. Why?

choices.A: Hydrochloric acid turns starch into glucose
choices.D: Salivary amylase breaks starch into sugar

questions.explanation: Amylase in saliva starts digesting starch to maltose, which tastes sweet.

questions.stem: A lack of which vitamin causes scurvy?
questions.explanation: Scurvy (bleeding gums) comes from too little vitamin C.

questions.stem: A food sample turns blue-black with iodine and stays blue after heating with Benedict's solution. It contains:
questions.explanation: Iodine is positive for starch; Benedict's stays blue when there is no reducing sugar.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is paired with the food class it digests?
questions.explanation: Lipase digests fats. Pepsin and trypsin digest protein, amylase digests starch.

questions.stem: Which statement about bile is correct?

choices.A: It is an enzyme that splits starch into maltose
choices.B: It emulsifies fat into small droplets, giving lipase a larger surface to work on
choices.D: It kills bacteria in the stomach with acid
choices.E: It is made in the gall bladder and stores glucose

questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and is not an enzyme.

questions.stem: A swimmer's meal: rice (starch), grilled chicken (protein) and olive oil (fat). Where does the first chemical digestion of each begin?

choices.A: All three begin in the stomach
choices.B: Protein in the mouth, starch in the stomach, fat in the small intestine
choices.C: Starch in the stomach, protein in the small intestine, fat in the mouth
choices.D: Fat in the stomach, starch in the small intestine, protein in the mouth
choices.E: Starch in the mouth, protein in the stomach, fat in the small intestine

questions.explanation: Amylase starts starch in the mouth, pepsin starts protein in the stomach, and bile with lipase start fat in the small intestine.

questions.stem: A swimmer takes a deep breath before pushing off the wall. Which muscle sheet below the lungs contracts to help her breathe in?
questions.explanation: The dome-shaped diaphragm contracts to draw air in.

questions.stem: In a swimmer's lungs, where does oxygen pass from the air into the blood?
questions.explanation: Alveoli have thin walls and are surrounded by capillaries.

questions.stem: Before a dive, a swimmer holds her breath. Which gas builds up in the blood and triggers the urge to breathe?
questions.explanation: Rising CO₂ is the main trigger for breathing.

questions.stem: During inhalation, which set of changes occurs?

choices.A: Diaphragm contracts, ribs move down, pressure in the lungs rises
choices.B: Diaphragm relaxes, ribs move up, pressure in the lungs falls
choices.C: The lungs expand by their own muscles and pull air in
choices.D: Diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs move up and out, pressure in the lungs falls
choices.E: Diaphragm relaxes and domes, ribs move down, pressure in the lungs rises

questions.explanation: A bigger chest volume lowers the pressure, so air flows in. Lungs have no muscles of their own.

questions.stem: Which feature does NOT help alveoli exchange gases efficiently?

choices.B: A very large total surface area

questions.explanation: Gases must diffuse through the wall, so it must be thin, not thick and muscular.

questions.stem: How are breathing and cellular respiration related?

choices.B: Breathing supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide so cells can carry out respiration
choices.C: Cellular respiration only occurs in the lungs
choices.D: Breathing takes place in the mitochondria
choices.E: Cellular respiration pumps air in and out of the lungs

questions.explanation: Breathing is a physical process; respiration is a chemical process in cells.

questions.stem: A person breathes out. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: Chest volume stays the same and the lungs squeeze air out
choices.B: Chest volume increases, so the pressure inside the lungs falls
choices.C: Chest volume increases, so the pressure inside the lungs rises
choices.D: Chest volume decreases, so the pressure inside the lungs falls below the outside pressure
choices.E: Chest volume decreases, so the pressure inside the lungs rises above the outside pressure

questions.explanation: Air always flows from high to low pressure. To leave the lungs, the pressure inside must be higher.

questions.stem: In a model of the chest, a balloon (lung) is inside a bottle with a rubber sheet (diaphragm) across the bottom. Pulling the sheet down makes the balloon:

choices.A: inflate, because the pressure in the bottle rises
choices.B: stay the same, because the bottle is sealed
choices.C: inflate, because the volume of the bottle increases and its pressure falls
choices.D: deflate, because the pressure in the bottle falls
choices.E: deflate, because the volume of the bottle increases

questions.explanation: Pulling the sheet down increases volume and lowers pressure around the balloon, so air from outside pushes in.

questions.stem: A chef filters stock to remove solids. In the body, which organ filters blood to make urine?
questions.explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons that filter the blood.

questions.stem: Which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?
questions.explanation: There is one ureter per kidney.

questions.stem: A swimmer blows bubbles underwater. Which gas is the main excretory product of the lungs?
questions.explanation: CO₂ from respiration is breathed out; water vapor is lost too.

questions.stem: A swimmer sweats while sitting by the pool on a hot day. What does sweat contain?

choices.C: Mostly water, with salts and a little urea

questions.explanation: Sweat is mostly water with dissolved salts and a little urea.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the path of urine out of the body?
questions.explanation: Urine is made in the kidneys, flows down the ureters, is stored in the bladder, and leaves via the urethra.

questions.stem: A cook eats a very protein-rich meal. Which organ converts the toxic ammonia from amino-acid breakdown into urea?
questions.explanation: The liver makes urea; the kidneys then remove it from the blood.

questions.stem: Which of these cannot pass through the kidney's filter, and so stays in the blood?
questions.explanation: Filtration lets small molecules through. Proteins and cells are too big.

questions.stem: Which statement about excretion is correct?

choices.A: Excretion only happens through the kidneys
choices.B: Excretion removes metabolic wastes made by cells, such as urea and carbon dioxide
choices.D: Feces are an excretory product of body cells
choices.E: Excretion removes undigested food from the gut

questions.explanation: Undigested food leaving the gut is egestion, not excretion. Wastes are also excreted by lungs and skin.

questions.stem: A swimmer must coordinate her arms and legs and stay balanced in the water. Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain controls heartbeat and breathing?
questions.explanation: The medulla controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing.

questions.stem: A player flicks the mouse the instant an enemy appears on screen. In this pathway, a sensory neuron carries impulses:

choices.A: from a muscle to a receptor
choices.B: only between the brain and the spinal cord
choices.C: from the receptor to the central nervous system
choices.E: from the CNS to a muscle

questions.explanation: Sensory neurons carry impulses toward the CNS.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of a reflex arc?

choices.A: Receptor → motor neuron → spinal cord → sensory neuron → effector
choices.B: Effector → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → receptor
choices.C: Sensory neuron → receptor → spinal cord → effector → motor neuron
choices.D: Receptor → sensory neuron → effector → spinal cord → motor neuron
choices.E: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector

questions.explanation: The stimulus is detected by a receptor, travels in, is relayed in the spinal cord, and leaves to an effector.

questions.stem: A swimmer steps on a hot pool deck and pulls her foot away before feeling pain. Why is this so fast?

choices.A: The muscles act on their own without nerves
choices.B: The reflex pathway goes through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain to decide
choices.C: Hormones carry the message to the leg
choices.D: Motor neurons are shorter than sensory neurons
choices.E: The brain sends faster signals than the spinal cord

questions.explanation: A reflex arc skips the thinking step, so the response is quicker. The brain feels the pain afterwards.

questions.stem: Which part of a neuron receives impulses from other neurons?
questions.explanation: Dendrites receive; the axon carries the impulse away.

questions.stem: A person has damaged only the motor neurons in a nerve of the arm; the sensory neurons are intact. What happens?

choices.A: Both feeling and movement are normal
choices.B: She can neither feel nor move the arm
choices.C: She can move the arm but cannot feel touch
choices.E: She can feel touch on the arm but cannot move its muscles

questions.explanation: Motor neurons carry commands to the muscles; sensory neurons carry feeling to the CNS.

questions.stem: In a motor neuron, in which direction does the impulse normally travel?

choices.A: Dendrites → cell body → axon → axon terminals
choices.B: Dendrites → axon terminals → axon → cell body
choices.C: Axon → dendrites → cell body → axon terminals
choices.D: Axon terminals → axon → cell body → dendrites
choices.E: Cell body → dendrites → axon → axon terminals

questions.explanation: Impulses enter at the dendrites, pass the cell body, run along the axon and exit at the terminals.

questions.stem: Which of these is part of innate immunity?
questions.explanation: Skin is a general barrier that is there from birth.

questions.stem: Which cells make antibodies?
questions.explanation: B cells turn into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

questions.stem: A dinner guest is allergic to shellfish. A substance such as shellfish protein that triggers an allergic reaction is called an:
questions.explanation: Common allergens are pollen, dust mites and some foods.

questions.stem: A child sneezes and gets hives after eating a little peanut butter. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: The peanut butter caused a bacterial infection
choices.B: The peanut permanently damages red blood cells
choices.C: The immune system overreacts to a harmless substance and releases histamine
choices.D: The child's immune system is too weak
choices.E: The reaction happens because the body lacks histamine

questions.explanation: An allergy is an immune overreaction to a harmless substance.

questions.stem: Why is a second infection by the same virus usually milder?

choices.C: Memory cells recognize it and respond faster
choices.D: Skin becomes thicker after the first infection
choices.E: Red blood cells carry more oxygen

questions.explanation: Adaptive immunity has memory.

questions.stem: What is the main job of killer T cells?

choices.B: To destroy body cells infected by viruses
choices.E: To engulf bacteria in the blood

questions.explanation: Killer (cytotoxic) T cells kill infected cells; B cells make antibodies.

questions.stem: Which statement about antibodies is correct?

choices.A: One type of antibody protects against all pathogens
choices.B: Each type of antibody fits one specific antigen
choices.E: Antibodies are made by T cells

questions.explanation: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins from B cells with specific binding sites.

questions.stem: How does a vaccine protect you?

choices.A: It directly kills the pathogen in the blood
choices.B: It exposes the immune system to a harmless form of the antigen so memory cells form without the disease
choices.C: It replaces your white blood cells
choices.E: It contains ready-made antibodies that last for life

questions.explanation: Vaccines trigger the adaptive response and memory cells. Giving ready-made antibodies is different, and short-lived.

questions.stem: A team captain directs the rest of the team. Which gland acts like that for the other endocrine glands (the 'master gland')?
questions.explanation: Its hormones control other glands.

questions.stem: A cook eats a sugary dessert. Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
questions.explanation: Insulin helps cells take up glucose.

questions.stem: Which gland makes thyroxine?
questions.explanation: Thyroxine, from the thyroid in the neck, sets the metabolic rate.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares endocrine and exocrine glands?

choices.A: Endocrine glands release products through ducts; exocrine glands release hormones into the blood
choices.B: Endocrine glands only exist in the brain
choices.C: Both release hormones directly into the blood
choices.D: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood; exocrine glands release products through ducts

questions.explanation: Sweat and salivary glands are exocrine; the thyroid is endocrine.

questions.stem: In a tense final round your heart pounds and your palms sweat. Which hormone from the adrenal glands is mainly responsible?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight.

questions.stem: The pancreas is:

choices.B: an exocrine gland that makes thyroxine
choices.D: both an exocrine gland (digestive juice) and an endocrine gland (insulin and glucagon)

questions.explanation: It has two jobs.

questions.stem: After a big pasta meal, blood glucose rises. What happens next?

choices.A: The pancreas releases insulin, and liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen
choices.B: The pancreas releases glucagon, and glycogen is broken down
choices.C: The adrenal glands release adrenaline to lower glucose
choices.D: The thyroid releases thyroxine to store glucose
choices.E: The pituitary stops all hormone release

questions.explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon does the opposite.

questions.stem: A person's diet lacks iodine for years. What is the most likely result?

choices.A: The pituitary stops making any hormone
choices.C: The thyroid enlarges (goiter) because it cannot make enough thyroxine
choices.D: The pancreas makes too much insulin

questions.explanation: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine.

questions.stem: A swimmer's muscles need extra blood in a sprint. Which heart chamber pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pushes blood into the aorta.

questions.stem: Which vessel carries blood from the heart to the body?
questions.explanation: The aorta is the largest artery.

questions.stem: Which blood group is the universal donor for red cells?
questions.explanation: Group O red cells have neither A nor B antigens.

questions.stem: During a sprint, a swimmer's heart rate rises. Which vessel returns oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium?
questions.explanation: The vena cava brings blood back from the body.

questions.stem: The pulmonary artery is unusual because it carries:

choices.D: oxygen-poor blood away from the heart to the lungs

questions.explanation: Arteries go away from the heart; the pulmonary artery is the exception that carries oxygen-poor blood.

questions.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?

choices.A: It pumps blood to the whole body at higher pressure; the right pumps only to the lungs
choices.D: It receives blood from the body

questions.explanation: A longer route needs a stronger pump.

questions.stem: A cook who eats a lot of salty food is at risk of hypertension. Which description fits hypertension?

choices.A: A fast pounding heartbeat that you can feel
choices.B: Blood pressure stays higher than normal
choices.E: A valve that does not close properly

questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest is a sudden stop; palpitations are felt beats.

questions.stem: A person has blood group A. Which red-cell groups can she safely receive?
questions.explanation: Her plasma has anti-B antibodies, so she cannot receive B or AB. A and O have no B antigen.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly follows blood leaving the left ventricle until it returns to the left ventricle?

choices.A: Aorta → lungs → pulmonary artery → right atrium → right ventricle → vena cava → body → pulmonary vein → left atrium
choices.B: Vena cava → body → aorta → left atrium → left ventricle → pulmonary vein → lungs → pulmonary artery → right atrium
choices.C: Aorta → body → vena cava → left atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → right atrium
choices.D: Aorta → body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium
choices.E: Aorta → body → pulmonary vein → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → vena cava → left atrium

questions.explanation: Systemic circuit (aorta, body, vena cava), then right heart, then pulmonary circuit (pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein) back to the left atrium.

questions.stem: Which statement about the lymphatic system is correct?

choices.A: It is pumped by the heart like arteries
choices.B: It is a closed loop with no connection to the blood
choices.C: Its vessels carry oxygen-rich red blood cells
choices.D: It carries urine away from the kidneys
choices.E: It returns excess tissue fluid to the blood and has nodes that help fight infection

questions.explanation: The lymphatic system runs parallel to the blood vessels and drains into the veins.

questions.stem: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living: temperature, light, water, soil, wind.

questions.stem: The lettuce in a salad makes its own food by photosynthesis. Organisms that do this are called:
questions.explanation: Producers are at the start of every food chain.

questions.stem: A mushroom grows on a dead log in the kitchen garden. It is a:
questions.explanation: Fungi break down dead matter and absorb the nutrients.

questions.stem: In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog is a:
questions.explanation: Grasshopper = primary, frog = secondary, snake = tertiary.

questions.stem: A tick feeds on the blood of a dog. This relationship is:
questions.explanation: The tick benefits and the dog is harmed, but the tick usually does not kill it.

questions.stem: What shape is a typical pyramid of numbers for grass → grasshopper → frog → snake?

choices.B: Narrow at the bottom and wide at the top
choices.C: A rectangle, with equal numbers at each level
choices.D: A diamond with the widest part in the middle
choices.E: Wide at the bottom and narrow at the top

questions.explanation: There are many more grass plants than snakes.

questions.stem: In a food web (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk; grass → mouse → snake; grass → rabbit → hawk) all the frogs disappear. Which is the most likely short-term effect?

choices.A: Rabbit numbers fall because snakes eat more rabbits
choices.B: Grasshopper numbers fall and the grass grows more
choices.C: Grasshopper numbers rise, and snakes eat more mice so mouse numbers may fall
choices.D: Nothing else in the web changes
choices.E: Hawks starve immediately because they eat frogs

questions.explanation: Fewer frogs means fewer grasshoppers eaten. Snakes lose one food source and rely more on mice. Hawks do not eat frogs and snakes do not eat rabbits.

questions.stem: A producer level holds 10 000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
questions.explanation: Primary consumers get 10% of 10 000 = 1000 kJ. Secondary consumers get 10% of 1000 = 100 kJ.

questions.stem: Chlorine is added to a swimming pool to kill bacteria. Which kingdom contains bacteria?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes, in kingdom Monera.

questions.stem: Amoeba belongs to which kingdom?
questions.explanation: Amoeba is a single-celled eukaryote.

questions.stem: A forgotten loaf grows a fuzzy green patch of mould. Which kingdom does bread mould belong to?
questions.explanation: Moulds are fungi.

questions.stem: An organism is multicellular, has cell walls of cellulose and makes food by photosynthesis. Which kingdom is it?
questions.explanation: These are the main features of plants.

questions.stem: Which feature is true of bacteria?

choices.C: Their cell walls are made of cellulose

questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes.

questions.stem: A pot of old bread grows a fuzzy mould. How does the mould get its food?

choices.A: By swallowing whole food with a mouth
choices.B: By making food from CO₂ and light
choices.D: Hyphae release enzymes and absorb the digested food

questions.explanation: Fungi are saprotrophs that feed by external digestion and absorption.

questions.stem: How does an Amoeba move and how does it reproduce?

choices.A: It moves with flagella and reproduces by budding
choices.B: It moves with pseudopodia and reproduces by spores
choices.C: It moves with cilia and reproduces by spores
choices.D: It moves with legs and reproduces by eggs
choices.E: It moves with pseudopodia and reproduces by binary fission

questions.explanation: Pseudopodia are temporary extensions of the cell.

questions.stem: Which kingdom and feature are correctly matched?

choices.B: Fungi – absorb food; cell walls contain chitin
choices.C: Animalia – cell walls made of cellulose
choices.E: Plantae – feed on dead matter; cell walls contain chitin

questions.explanation: Fungal cell walls contain chitin.

questions.stem: Which pair consists of two invertebrates?
questions.explanation: Invertebrates have no backbone. Frogs, sharks, lizards and dolphins are vertebrates.
